summary:
Same-sex relations are not criminalised in Cabo Verde. The employment discrimination prohibition covers sexual orientation but does not extend to gender identity, leaving trans workers without an explicit statutory basis for workplace complaints (Outright International, updated 12 March 2026).

No legal gender recognition framework is on record. As of 2016 civil law blocked Tchinda Andrade, the first publicly self-outed trans woman in Cabo Verde, from changing her legal name to a female one; the source inventory contains no later statute or administrative route for legal gender change.

Trans visibility carries a documented violence risk. Tchinda Andrade, who came out publicly in 1997 at the age of 19, reported verbal abuse and two physical attacks, while describing Cabo Verde as markedly freer for LGBT people than other African countries and the island of São Vicente as relaxed (Rede Angola interview, 22 June 2016).

Same-sex unions are not recognised. Prime Minister Ulisses Correia e Silva stated on 11 July 2017 that same-sex marriage was not on the government's agenda, following LGBT community demands for civil unions and marriage.

Public visibility is high and civic registration is open. LGBTIQ organisations register freely, and the first public Pride was held in 2013, making Cabo Verde the second African country to stage one. The 2018 Pride Week in Praia combined a parade with campaigns by Associação Gay de Cabo Verde, Associação LGBTI de Praia and Associação Arco Iris petitioning the National Assembly for same-sex marriage and an anti-discrimination law, with the state gender-equality institute ICIEG and UN Women engaged in the programme.

Protection machinery exists alongside the legal gaps. Polling across 2019–21 found that 82% of respondents would accept a 'homosexual' neighbour, Cabo Verde is one of two African members of the UN LGBTI Core Group, and the country made anti-discrimination commitments in its 2024 Universal Periodic Review.
tangentialFactors:
Afrobarometer Dispatch No. 362 (May 2020) reports that Africans are tolerant on ethnic, religious and national differences but not on sexual differences, and identifies Cabo Verde, Namibia and São Tomé and Príncipe as particularly tolerant countries. The same survey finds tolerance toward sexual minorities remaining remarkably weak even among younger respondents, which qualifies the 82% neighbour-acceptance figure recorded in 2019–21.

The prime minister's 2017 remark was made while distancing himself from opposition voiced by MpD secretary-general Miguel Monteiro, indicating that party-level positions were more hostile than the government's stated agenda at the time.

Cabo Verde's standing is repeatedly framed comparatively: the second African country to hold a public Pride, one of two African members of the UN LGBTI Core Group, and one of three African countries singled out for tolerance by Afrobarometer. Comparative standing of this kind does not alter the absence of a legal gender recognition route or of union recognition.

The 2018 petition to the National Assembly sought an anti-discrimination law broader than the sexual-orientation-only employment provision then in force, so the legislative gap being pressed by residents' organisations was current as of July 2018.
localsOnly:
Residents have an explicit statutory basis for workplace complaints on grounds of sexual orientation, but no equivalent gender-identity ground; the employment protection does not reach gender identity (Outright International, 12 March 2026).

Legal gender change was unavailable in 2016 and no successor route appears in the source inventory, affecting identity documents and the name a resident carries in everyday dealings.

Residents cannot enter a recognised same-sex union. Community organisations pressed for civil unions and marriage ahead of the prime minister's July 2017 statement that the issue was off the government's agenda.

Civic space is open: LGBTIQ organisations register without restriction, Pride has run since 2013, and the 2018 Pride Week in Praia drew in ICIEG and UN Women alongside Associação Gay de Cabo Verde, Associação LGBTI de Praia and Associação Arco Iris. Cabo Verde sits in the UN LGBTI Core Group with one other African state and filed anti-discrimination commitments in the 2024 Universal Periodic Review.

Documented hostility toward trans residents is personal rather than institutional in the sourced record: Tchinda Andrade reported verbal violence and two physical attacks after coming out in 1997, in a country she described as relaxed by regional standards.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory carries no source on hate-crime provisions or on whether violence motivated by gender identity is prosecuted. The two physical attacks reported by Tchinda Andrade in her 2016 interview have no recorded complaint, arrest or court outcome, so their disposition remains unresolved.

No source addresses legal gender recognition after 2016. Whether an administrative route, a court petition or a later statute opened a route to change legal sex or first name is unresolved in this inventory; the record simply contains nothing after the 2016 civil-law refusal.

Entry and border screening of trans travellers is not sourced here: no material covers visa or arrival document checks, gender markers on passports presented at Cabo Verdean entry, or whether travellers are questioned about gender presentation. Nothing in the inventory should be read as a finding on entry rules.

Access to trans-specific healthcare, screening programmes and facility rules such as gendered bathrooms or changing areas are not covered by any source supplied, and are not evidenced either way.

Enforcement of the sexual-orientation employment protection is unsourced: there are no complaint statistics, labour-inspectorate findings or case reports in the inventory.

The outcome of the 2018 National Assembly petition for same-sex marriage and a general anti-discrimination law is not stated in the sources, so whether either measure advanced or stalled after July 2018 is unresolved.
